attempts.result: every capture stopped at the 1200 s readiness wait: /health stayed 'loading' while CUDA graphs were captured under ncu; unit memory reached the 36 GiB cap

attempts.mode: eager decode (--cuda-graph-max-bs 0, same kernels), --profile-from-start off, window cudaProfilerStart/Stop around the measured requests, kernel filter from the nsys private targets, sections SpeedOfLight/MemoryWorkloadAnalysis/ComputeWorkloadAnalysis/Occupancy/LaunchStats, launch-count 1, 15 min limit per capture
attempts.result: stopped after the first capture by design (hang, no new attempts)
diagnosis: server loaded in ~1.5 min and logged 'CUDA graph is disabled' and 'API server is ready' (the graph-capture hang is gone)
during the remaining 13 minutes the unit's journal shows 0 prefill/decode batches: no request reached the model, so the profile window never opened and ncu reported 'No kernels were profiled'
profile-request.py run printed neither an error nor a receipt, i.e. the client did not get past its start-up phase (health wait / request build) before the 900 s limit
unit CPU time 13 min over 15 min wall: the model process stays busy under ncu interception (16 MoE CPU threads, host-side expert/LRU work) while idle

unverified hypotheses: (a) /health is served through the engine process and does not answer while ncu intercepts its launches; (b) the client blocks in the tokenizer/bench import. A 2-minute dry run of profile-request.py run with strace/py-spy against an ncu-attached server, or starting ncu with --target-processes application-only on the engine worker, would separate them.

attempts.mode: observation only (no kernel capture): eager decode under ncu with the real client wrapped in faulthandler, /health sampled every 10 s, thread CPU sampled, plus an ncu launch-overhead microbench
findings: /health answers in 2-3 ms throughout: 'loading' for ~100 s after the unit start (model load under ncu), then 'ok'; it is not the blocker

profile-request.py run is not stuck at start-up: faulthandler dumps taken at 45 s intervals show it first in wait_health, later in the blocking read of the chunked HTTP response of the first request, i.e. the request was sent and no response arrives
the server process stays at ~760-790 % CPU (R state) and ncu at ~90 % of one core for the whole 5.5 min; no batch completes

ncu per-launch cost, measured with the capture's flags and a filter that matches nothing: 50-57 us per kernel launch vs 6 us without ncu (3000 launches); the plan has ~490k kernel launches, so interception overhead alone is ~25 s, not the 15 min seen
the earlier 'No kernels were profiled' is consistent with the launch-skip ordinals (7k-14k launches of the target kernel) never being reached
attempts.conclusion: cause not established; the remaining hypothesis is that ncu serialises kernel execution and the model has kernels that wait for concurrent work (copy stream, mapped-host gather, decode overlap), so the run livelocks; this needs ptrace-level tools (py-spy/strace/gdb as root) that this user session does not have (ptrace_scope=1, py-spy and strace not installed)
attempts.recommendation: component-level ncu of the kernels (kernels/*/bench scripts, as in results/nsight/ncu-component-kernels.json) for L0 vs L9 equivalents; no further model-level attempts without root-level tracing

available_compute_evidence: results/nsight/ncu-component-kernels.json (component-level ncu of the kernels, not the model process)
